Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. ## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.

- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# A thin wrapper: every decision lives in the engine modules named in the `run:`
# lines below, which converge nightly — this file does not, so it must not grow
# logic. This copy is hand-maintained — the canon has no converge — so it is
# edited in the same commit as the stub beside it.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      continuation_depth:
        description: 'How many dead runs this chain has continued through — set by the continuation job below, never by hand'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  execute:
    # A workflow's event trigger names label strings LITERALLY — nothing here
    # decodes. The legacy `task:ready` stood beside this one while a fielded engine
    # could still write it; no member stamps such a version any more (#1119).
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:status:waiting-for-executor'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # A backstop against a wedged runner, well clear of any declared
    # `code_work_timeout`; the heartbeat's leash is what bounds real work.
    timeout-minutes: 350
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Pick up and execute ready work
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}
          # Every declared task's `required_secrets`, plus the configured endpoint
          # tokens, regenerated by the wiring converge. Actions requires each secret
          # to be named statically, so this list is the whole delivery mechanism; a
          # worker then reads process.env.<NAME>.
          #
          # The converge writes the list directly beneath this line, so it stays last.
          # claudinite:secrets
          # Hand-maintained here: this list is what the marker above produces on a
          # member. The canon has no converge of its own to regenerate it.
          FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
          CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
        run: node packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/executor.mjs

  continue-the-chain:
    needs: execute
    if: failure() || cancelled()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Continue the drain, or escalate a chain that keeps dying
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          CLAUDINITE_CONTINUATION_DEPTH: ${{ inputs.continuation_depth }}
        run: node packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/executor-continuation.mjs

    Name the executor's secrets again; `toJSON(secrets)` is what GitHub flags (#1337)
    
    Reverses #1301's one-line secret bag, on the owner's call.
    
    The line `CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}` is the shape GitHub's
    malicious-workflow detection flags. A flagged workflow does not run until a
    person clicks Approve, and it parks with zero jobs — so from the queue's side it
    is indistinguishable from "nothing was pickable". An unattended fleet can
    neither absorb that nor notice it. It began two minutes after #1302 merged and
    had been silently eating executor runs in the canon and in Shepherd since.
    
    So the executor workflow lists each secret again, and the wiring converge — now
    the tasks pack's converge-workflows.mjs — regenerates that list at the
    `# claudinite:secrets` marker from every declared task's `required_secrets` plus
    the configured endpoint tokens.
    
    The cost this reinstates is the one #1301 removed and is not pretended away: the
    file becomes a function of the task set, `.github/workflows/` is the one path a
    converge cannot write, and a NEW secret therefore needs a human-merged PR in
    every member — the coupling that wedged one in #1296. The trade is deliberate: a
    rare human-merged PR beats a permanent human click on every run.
    
    secrets-bag.mjs stays. Its selection — a task's code-work sees exactly the names
    its own declaration lists, rather than inheriting the executor's whole
    environment — was #1301's other half, it is independent of how the secrets
    arrive, and it keeps working off the plain environment. Its bag reader stays too,

{"number":1336,"title":"GitHub flags the executor workflow as malicious: `toJSON(secrets)` parks every run until a human approves it","body":"Every member's executor workflow is now one workflow-file change away from being parked by GitHub with:

> GitHub detected that this workflow file may be malicious. It will not run until someone with write access approves it.

A parked run creates **zero jobs** and concludes `action_required` in about a second, so from the queue's side the item simply never gets picked up — no error, no failure, nothing red. It reads exactly like a settings problem, which is how I first mis-diagnosed it in #1330.

## What triggers it

`packs/claudinite-tasks/stubs/claudinite-executor.yml:52`, and the canon's own copy at the same line:

```yaml
CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}
```

Serialising the entire secrets context into an environment variable is the canonical exfiltration shape, and GitHub's malicious-workflow detection flags it. (The banner does not name the line; that it is this one is inferred from the timing below plus the pattern being the only thing in the file that fits.)

## The timing, which is unambiguous

| When (UTC) | What |
|---|---|
| 2026-08-24 06:07:55 | Claudinite's executor — last `success` |
| 2026-08-24 08:31:14 | `fd4cb68` merges #1302, adding the `toJSON(secrets)` line |
| 2026-08-24 08:33:31 | Claudinite's executor — first `action_required`, two minutes later |
| 2026-08-24 11:24, 11:27 | Shepherd's executor — `success`, twice |
| 2026-08-24 11:48 onward | Shepherd's executor — `action_required` on every run, bot- and owner-triggered alike |

**This predates the #1317 extraction and is unrelated to it.** The extraction carried the line forward unchanged, which was right — but see the L2 consequence below.

## Why it matters more than one approval

- The line is in the **stub every member is scaffolded with**, so this is not two repos, it is the fleet.
- The whole point of the queue is unattended work. A gate that needs a person to press *Approve and run* is the one thing the mechanism cannot absorb.
- It is **silent**. `action_required` with zero jobs is indistinguishable from "nothing was pickable" unless you go looking at run conclusions, and the fleet's own health signals read stamps, not run states.
- **#1317's L2 (#1331) will trip it on all 14 members.** L2 hand-edits both workflow files in every member; each edit re-exposes the file to the scan. That turns a per-repo mechanical edit into a per-repo edit *plus* a manual approval, and any member missed sits with a stalled queue and nothing red to show for it.

## What #1302 was solving, and a shape that keeps it

#1302's problem was real: naming secrets one by one meant every new secret needed a human-merged PR in every member, and `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push. Reverting reinstates exactly that.

Three ways out, in the order I'd weigh them:

1. **One dedicated secret holding a JSON blob.** The workflow line becomes `CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ secrets.CLAUDINITE_SECRETS }}` — static, no `toJSON`, and still one line that never changes when a task needs a new value, because the value lives inside that one secret rather than in the YAML. Keeps #1302's property and drops the flagged pattern.
2. **Name the secrets explicitly again.** Safe, and gives back the fleet-wide-PR-per-secret cost #1302 removed.
3. **Keep it and absorb the approvals.** Cheapest today, and it makes an unattended fleet depend on someone noticing a silent park.

Option 1 needs checking against what `secrets-bag.mjs` actually reads before it is more than a sketch.

## GitHub Actions Secret Exfiltration Using toJSON Pattern

The "toJSON(secrets)" pattern sits quietly in an environment variable as part of recent malicious GitHub Actions workflows designed to exfiltrate secrets. 

StepSecurity now blocks and detects secret exfiltration in GitHub Actions, stopping attacks that plant malicious workflows to steal repository secrets.

Secrets can be dumped using the secrets context, toJson(secrets) & variable names with the vars context and GitHub's built-in toJson() function. This demonstrates how the `toJSON` function is specifically used as a technique in secret exfiltration attacks.

## False Positive Detection Challenge

The challenge with detecting these attacks is that every line is designed to look ordinary—the workflow name and step name read as routine tooling, the actions/checkout and actions/upload-artifact steps are pinned to commit SHAs like any hardened workflow, and the only line that matters, toJSON(secrets), sits quietly in an environment variable.

This is why such patterns can trigger false positives in security scanning—legitimate uses of `toJSON` exist in workflows, making it difficult for automated detection tools to distinguish between benign and malicious uses without additional context.

content.text:
## Short answer

Almost certainly no — and we already ship `toJSON(vars)` in the fleet without incident.

## What actually got flagged

[#1336](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1336) → [#1337](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1337). The line was:

```yaml
CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}
```

Two minutes after it merged, every executor run started parking `action_required` with zero jobs. That's GitHub's [malicious-workflow hold](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-28-github-actions-holds-potentially-malicious-workflows-for-approval/), shipped 2026-07-28, automatic, public repos on github.com only, cleared only by a write-access human in an authenticated web session.

## Why `vars` is a different case

**1. The detector's threat model is credential theft.** The changelog's stated motivation is "compromised GitHub credentials … that steal CI/CD credentials." Serializing the whole `secrets` context into an env var is the canonical exfiltration primitive. `vars` is, per GitHub's own docs, the context that structurally cannot carry a credential:

> Variables provide a way to store and reuse **non-sensitive** configuration information. […] **Warning:** By default, variables render unmasked in your build outputs. If you need greater security for sensitive information, such as passwords, use secrets instead.

Dumping a context GitHub itself renders unmasked in logs is not an exfiltration signal — there is nothing to exfiltrate.

**2. It's a mainstream, tooled-for pattern.** `${{ toJSON(vars) }}` is the documented way to hand all repo variables to a step; there are [Marketplace actions built specifically to consume it](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/export-a-key-value-pair-json-to-env-variables) and a [long-standing community discussion](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/47165) recommending it. Flagging it would be a mass false-positive event, not a quiet one.

**3. We are already running it.** The `static-website` pack's stubs pass exactly this, in two workflows:

- `packs/static-website/stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml:62`
- `packs/static-website/stubs/workflows/static-site-deploy-pages.yml:70`

Both predate the detection rollout and neither has produced a park. The pack even states the reasoning at `read-config.mjs:41` — *"`toJSON(vars)`, a context that structurally cannot carry a secret."*

## The caveats worth carrying

- **GitHub publishes no signals, thresholds or false-positive rate.** This is inference from the threat model, the docs and our own field evidence — not a guarantee. The classifier is opaque and can change without a changelog entry.
- **Failure mode is still silent.** If it ever did fire, we'd get the same zero-job `action_required` that reads as "nothing was pickable" — which is what cost us a mis-diagnosis in [#1330](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1330).
- **Our own guard wouldn't catch it.** `packs/claudinite-tasks/test/converge-workflows.test.mjs:163` pins only `toJSON(secrets)` out of the stubs.

## The shape that makes the question moot

If the motivation is the [#1337](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1337) coupling — a new value meaning a human-merged PR in every member, since a converge can't write `.github/workflows/` — there's a strictly better move for vars than for secrets:

```yaml
CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_VARS }}   # one static line, forever
```

with the JSON blob living inside that one variable. This is option 1 from [#1336](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1336), except that for **variables it fully closes** — repo variables are API-writable (`PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/variables/{name}`, [fine-grained "Variables" repository permission, write](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/actions/variables)). So the converge can maintain the blob itself, unattended, with no human anywhere in the loop and no exposure to the detector. That's more than `toJSON(vars)` would buy, since `toJSON(vars)` still requires someone to have set each variable per repo.

Cost: `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` (or whatever writes it) needs the Variables:write scope, and the blob becomes a single opaque value rather than N inspectable ones.

> ✅ Researched, no changes made. `toJSON(vars)` is very unlikely to be flagged — different threat model, mainstream pattern, and we already field it in the `static-website` stubs. But if the goal is removing the human-merged-PR-per-value coupling, a single `CLAUDINITE_VARS` blob written by the converge over the REST API beats it outright and sidesteps the opaque classifier entirely. Say the word and I'll spec that.

input.title: The executor carries repo variables as one `toJSON(vars)` bag
input.body:
A task that needs a repository **variable** today pays what a task needing a **secret** pays: the executor workflow must name it statically, `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot write, so a new value needs a human-merged PR in every member — the coupling that wedged one in #1296.

For secrets that cost was taken back deliberately in #1336/#1337, because the one-line alternative, `toJSON(secrets)`, is the shape GitHub's [malicious-workflow detection](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-28-github-actions-holds-potentially-malicious-workflows-for-approval/) flags: every run parks with zero jobs until a person clicks Approve, silently.

**That reasoning does not carry to `vars`.**

- The safeguard's stated threat model is credential theft. `vars` is the context GitHub's own docs define as non-sensitive — *"Variables provide a way to store and reuse non-sensitive configuration information […] By default, variables render unmasked in your build outputs. If you need greater security for sensitive information, such as passwords, use secrets instead."* Dumping a context GitHub already renders unmasked in logs is not an exfiltration signal.
- `${{ toJSON(vars) }}` is a mainstream pattern with Marketplace actions built to consume it. Flagging it would be a mass false-positive event.
- **We already field it.** `packs/static-website/stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml:62` and `static-site-deploy-pages.yml:70` both pass `REPO_VARS_JSON: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}`, and have since before the safeguard shipped. No park. `read-config.mjs:41` already states the reasoning: *"`toJSON(vars)`, a context that structurally cannot carry a secret."*

## The change

One static line in the executor's work step, never regenerated, never a function of the task set:

```yaml
CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}
```

- A reader beside `secrets-bag.mjs`, sharing its bag mechanics rather than copying them, with the same fall-back-to-plain-env posture that makes the pre-PR window uneventful.
- `taskEnv` unpacks it, so a task's code-work reads `process.env.<NAME>` for any repo variable with nothing naming it in YAML. Unlike the secrets bag there is no per-task selection: vars are non-sensitive by construction, so the blast-radius argument that justified `required_secrets` has nothing to bite on.
- The scheduler stub is untouched. It runs no task code, and its one named variable is the operator hold, which every entry point must read before any bag exists.
- The `toJSON(secrets)` guard stays exactly as strict, and gains a sibling asserting the vars line IS present.

## Caveat carried in the code, not just here

GitHub publishes no detection signals, thresholds or false-positive rate. This is inference from the threat model, the docs and our own field evidence — not a guarantee. If it ever did fire, the failure mode is the silent `action_required` park that cost a mis-diagnosis in #1330.

Refs #1336

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if

7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,

   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

# The CANON repo's own CI — Claudinite's test suite + its own conformance sweep
# on every PR. Not consumer wiring (consumers ship no workflow, #385).
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  # Dispatchable so a GITHUB_TOKEN-authored PR (whose push/open GitHub never
  # turns into a pull_request run — the recursion guard) can still get this
  # suite started on its branch: baselining's deliver() and any bot-authored
  # PR flow (#432, #565) dispatch it explicitly.
  workflow_dispatch:
defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash
jobs:
  test-and-conformance:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          # Check out the PR's real head, not the synthetic refs/pull/N/merge commit
          # actions/checkout uses by default — otherwise HEAD is an ephemeral merge of
          # the branch into main, which the work-scoped squash-merge-history check would
          # (correctly, for that synthetic commit) flag. This makes CI evaluate exactly
          # what the local Stop hook does: the branch tip. Falls back to github.sha on push.
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Unit tests
        # THE test roots — a closed set of FOLDERS, each swept to any depth. Depth is
        # deliberately not enumerated: the previous form spelled out one glob per level of
        # nesting, so a test at an unlisted depth was silently never run — which is exactly
        # how vendoring/'s two files sat outside CI. `**` removes depth from the question;
        # what remains is the root list, and engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs fails the
        # moment a tracked test lands outside it. Adding a root is a deliberate CI edit;
        # adding a test is not.
        #   engine-tests/            engine/ (migrations included) + the other top-level canon code;
        #                            mirrors engine/'s inner structure, and stays canon-side
        #                            because engine/ ships to consumers exactly as-is (#385)
        #   packs/                   every canon pack's tests, each inside the pack it covers
        #   vendoring/               co-located with the vendor computer/writer they cover,
        #                            the fixture-consumer rehearsal included
        #   dev/tools/               maintainer-side tooling nothing at session time runs
        #   .claudinite/local/packs/ this repo's own local packs — tests live inside the tree
        # nullglob: a root with no tests drops out instead of reaching node as a literal pattern.
        run: |
          shopt -s globstar nullglob
          tests=(engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs/**/*.test.mjs vendoring/**/*.test.mjs dev/tools/**/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs)
          # Deliberately oversubscribed. node --test defaults to one worker per core
          # minus one, which fits a CPU-bound suite; this one spends most of its wall
          # clock waiting — on git plumbing, spawned workers and converge fixtures — so
          # the cores idle at that default (measured on this tree: 106s wall against
          # 187s of user+sys on 4 cores). Doubling the workers: 106s -> 70s, with 16
          # buying only another 2s.
          #
          # TAP goes to a FILE, not the log. 2,448 tests emit ~13,000 lines at 5.3
          # lines each, and a failing run's one `not ok` sits wherever its file

          # blob URL that would serve the whole thing is proxy-blocked. So a red run

          # name the test (#1170). Printing the failing blocks puts the identity in
          # the tail, where it can actually be read.
          status=0
          node --test --test-concurrency=$(( $(nproc) * 2 )) "${tests[@]}" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/tests.tap" || status=$?

            echo '::group::failing tests'
            grep -n -A 25 '^not ok' "$RUNNER_TEMP/tests.tap" || echo 'no `not ok` line — the runner died before reporting one'
            echo '::endgroup::'
          fi
          tail -n 12 "$RUNNER_TEMP/tests.tap"
          exit "$status"

        # from the repo root instead of the mount.
        #
        # --branch explicitly: the checkout above is a detached head at the PR's real
